description_full: FormFactor, Inc. designs, manufactures, and sells probe cards, analytical probes, probe stations, thermal systems, cryogenic systems, and related services in the United States, South Korea, Taiwan, China, Japan, Singapore, Europe, Malaysia, and internationally. It operates in two segments: Probe Cards and Systems segments. The company provides probe cards to test various semiconductor device types, including systems- on-chip products, such as graphics, central, digital processing units, and other custom application-specific processing units; mobile application processors, microprocessors, and microcontrollers; network devices, which include switches and network processing units; dynamic random-access memory; radio-frequency amplifiers and filters; antenna-in-package devices; analog and mixed-signal integrated circuits; image sensors; co-packaged optical integrated circuits; NAND flash memory; NOR flash memory; and quantum computer processor devices. It also offers analytical probes, which are used for device characterization, electrical simulation model development, failure analysis, and prototype design debugging; probe stations, a critical tool for the development of new generations of semiconductor and electro-optical processes and designs; and thermal subsystems, which include thermal chucks and other test systems used in probe stations and other applications for precise temperature management. In addition, the company provides cryogenic systems, which includes the manufacture of precision cryogenic instruments and semiconductor test and measurement systems; and services and support, including installation services. Further, it offers on-site probe card maintenance and service training, seminars, and telephone support services. It sells its products through direct sales force, manufacturers' representatives, and distributors. It has a strategic collaboration with Teradyne. The company was incorporated in 1993 and is headquartered in Livermore, California.

financial_summary: FormFactor, Inc. is a mid-cap technology business with a $6.4B market cap on $785M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +11% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory. Operating margins are expanding by +3.5pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 9% against a 12% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 39%.

The business throws off $12M in free cash flow — roughly 1 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.12× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 0.4%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 7% operating margin is roughly in line with the Technology median (7%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.31x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-20.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 161% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 38% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 49% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 87% and a beta of 1.38, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 2.75 vs 5y 1.71), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $140.8M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 41% in the 2020 crash, 61% in the 2022 bear market and 64% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $13.76 (margin of safety -489%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 11%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $8.77 to $22.72 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: P/E 37.2 vs 26.7, EV/EBITDA 20.9 vs 16.4 and P/FCF 541.7 vs 25.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 158% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 0.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 1.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 9 covering analysts target $152 on average, 88% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 9% falls short of the cost of capital of 11.6%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 159.35).
It runs a 39% gross margin and converts 1% of revenue into free cash flow, or -3% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.12x.
ROE of 5% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 14.7% of revenue on R&D and 4.9% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $263.0M (1% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 21.6, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.6% over 3 years, 2.5% over 5 years and 10.8% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 15%).
At current returns, reinvesting 55% of profits supports about 5.2% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -36.5% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.01, a backlog worth 4% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 6%.
Capex runs 2.8x depreciation (13.2% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.7%), and institutions hold 94%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (30 sales, net $9.6M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.4% (0.4% in buybacks).
people: With about 2,153 employees, each generates about $365K of revenue, in line with the Technology median, and productivity has risen 11.6% a year.
That works out to $5K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.1M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
